findings.claim: Salted water & the float test, the bare simmer and blanching & shocking are one lesson at three heats
findings.because: Two of the three run at the same heat. The brief's marks for salted water want a pot that "returns to its boil quickly after the food goes in and never stops moving", and blanching wants "a large volume at a hard rolling boil"; only the bare simmer sits below the boil. Two heats, not three.
findings.fix: Salted water & the float test, blanching & shocking and the bare simmer are one lesson at two heats, the rolling boil and the shiver under it:

findings.claim: learn which before anything else here
findings.because: Paragraph 1 has already said "Take the board first." A cook reading both is told two different first things. The brief's definition only says knowing which of the three verbs a recipe means is the difference between following recipes and cooking.
findings.fix: learn which before you take any pan further

findings.claim: are dry heat at three distances
findings.because: Distance is not what separates them: the brief's charring standard names "flame, a broiler, or bare hot metal" as charring's own heat, and roasting is "dry ambient heat in an enclosed oven" while the broiler is "top-down radiant heat". What differs is where the heat comes from.
findings.fix: are dry heat from three directions: all around, from above, and straight against the surface

findings.claim: come down to full commitment, then drying the surface before heat
findings.because: "Fully committed either way" is brining & curing's mark alone. Salting to draw the water out is met on different marks: salted evenly over every surface, laid out so the water has somewhere to go (a colander, a rack, a sieve over a bowl), visible liquid to show for it, and that liquid squeezed, blotted or poured away. As written the reader would salt and wait and never pour the water off.
findings.fix: come down to salt on every face, somewhere for the water to go, that water poured off, and the surface dry before heat

findings.claim: work down it in the order above
findings.because: The order above leaves out eight techniques placed at this level, several among the most used here: Straining & passing through a sieve (148 recipes), Steaming: basket, leaf and lid (130), Mashing & puréeing (114), Frying the paste until the oil splits (95), Dry-pan toasting: spices, seeds and nuts (70), Soaking dried goods back to life (69), Egg wash & the baker's shine (34) and Dashi (29). A cook following the order as given would meet the index and find work it never mentioned.
findings.fix: work down it in the order above, then take the pot's other work as recipes call for it: soaking dried goods, steaming, straining & passing through a sieve, mashing & puréeing, dashi, frying the paste until the oil splits, dry-pan toasting and egg wash

Paragraph 1: "These are the deck's first cards, one to a menu word." The subset counts "the twenty methods" and "the nine menu words" are exact and can stay.

problems.issue: Rule 11 is broken in three places. The lede says "Three folios", paragraph 1 says "Commis holds three of them" (the level's own count), and next says "Chef de Partie hangs sixteen folios" (the next level's count).
problems.fix: Lede: "Folios for the first weeks: the chicken on your board, the spices in their whole form and the mushrooms in the walk-in, six subjects to each." Paragraph 1: "Commis holds Chicken: cuts and giblets, Spices: from fruit to flower and Mushrooms: six cultivated market forms." Next: "Chef de Partie hangs the folios for pork and beef, the Pacific, Atlantic and Gulf Coast fish cases, the vegetables and fruits of five regions, and cheese read through its milk, make and maturation."

problems.issue: Rule 11: paragraph 1 says "Six items sit here and they fold into four ideas", which is a count of the subsection's items.
problems.fix: Change it to "The items here fold into four ideas: the danger zone, the two-hour rule, cross-contamination and FIFO." Keep "four ideas", because that is a named grouping and not the item count.

problems.issue: Rule 11: paragraph 1 opens "Service at Commis is four modules in two pairs", a count of the level's items. Paragraph 6 also calls the cross-subsection test "The Commis test", but the brief's levelTest names it "the Level test at the foot of the level page", and the dishes and lexicon primers both call it the Level test. A reader sees two names for one door.
problems.fix: Paragraph 1: "Service at Commis runs in two pairs." and keep the rest of that paragraph. In paragraph 6, delete the last sentence about the test; the Level test is now covered once, in the dishes primer (see the 1-lexicon problem). "The track, all 27 modules" can stay, because that is the door's own label.

problems.issue: Paragraph 4 restates the repair table's levers: salt first and acid second for flat; dilute, or bulk with starch or cream, for salty. That is the whole job of the 1-palate primer, which gives the full order (salt, acid, umami; dilute, bulk, counter). Read side by side, the lexicon version stops early: it drops umami and the counter lever, so the two readers look like they disagree.
problems.fix: Keep the group (Tasting & Seasoning Like a Chef, Salt & Perception, The Repair Table) and the sentence "Taste at every stage and season in layers." Replace the two lever sentences with one pointer: "The Palate on this page puts the repair table's first two faults on a plate, lever by lever; here you learn the words your chef will use at the pass when a plate comes back."

problems.issue: Three primers describe the same Level test. Dishes (paragraph 6), lexicon (paragraph 5) and service (paragraph 6) each describe it as untimed, across every subsection, ending on what you missed. A cook reading down the page meets the same sentence three times.
problems.fix: Delete the last sentence of lexicon paragraph 5 ("When the words feel like yours, the Level test ... with the right answers."). Keep the description only in 1-dishes paragraph 6, which is the first primer on the page, and remove the service sentence as noted under 1-service.

Put beside 1-plates, that reads as a contradiction: the Commis plate Spices: from fruit to flower teaches cumin, coriander, cinnamon, turmeric and cloves. A cook sees cumin placed at Commis in one primer and at Chef de Partie in another.
problems.fix: Name the spice rack with Lexicon entries the Commis folio does not show, for example: "...baking science in Gluten & Hydration and Chemical Leaveners; and the spice rack in depth, from Saffron and Sichuan Peppercorn & Málà to Garam Masala." All three are in the brief's neighbours.above names.

critic.notes: I did not raise these, because the overlap is by design. (1) Blanching and shocking, sweat/sauté/sear, and watching the bubble are glossed in dishes, techniques and lexicon alike. Each gloss does its own subsection's job (why the dish asks for it, the mark to meet, the word's definition), and they agree with each other. Only the lexicon repair-table passage duplicates another primer's whole job, and that one is listed above. (2) The same name appears at two levels across subsections. Hollandaise and Crème Brûlée are Commis deck cards but show up in the Chef de Partie next lines for techniques and dishes, and \"Braised\" is a Commis card while braising is a Chef de Partie technique, dish and Lexicon entry. This follows the written standard (Commis knows the word a guest assumes; Chef de Partie cooks it), so it is not a primer error. If the owner wants a cook to see why, the level page could say once that the deck places the menu word while the techniques place the cooking. (3) The 1-dishes and 1-lexicon primers were not on disk (tools/derive/primers holds only deck, palate, plates, safety, service and techniques for Commis), so I read them from the task text. (4) The deck primer is 557 words, above the 520 aim and inside the 650 limit. The deletions above bring it closer.
